narrative_idea_gen: Grigori Plink, a catastrophically clumsy counterfeiter in a provincial town where every building smells of boiled cabbage and thwarted ambition, keeps literally crashing into — through doors, down staircases, off a municipal balcony — the new forensic documents clerk, Yevgenia, who has been assigned to analyze his laughably obvious forged tax stamps, and who finds his particular brand of physical destruction inexplicably, infuriatingly charming. Told entirely through Grigori's myopic, bruise-cataloguing perspective, the story follows their escalating courtship conducted across crime scenes and bureaucratic offices, each romantic milestone punctuated by some grotesque slapstick catastrophe — their first kiss interrupted when he tumbles backward through a filing cabinet full of evidence against him, their secret wedding reception ending with him face-first in the civil registrar's ink pot — until his forgeries accidentally expose a massive pension fraud by the town's beloved deputy governor, briefly making Grigori a folk hero celebrated at a banquet where the mayor herself pins a medal on his chest. But the same exposure that elevated him reveals Yevgenia's complicity in concealing his crimes, and the town's bureaucratic machinery — which only ever loved the *idea* of an honest man — grinds them both into nothing: she is transferred to a records office in a city no one can find on a map, and Grigori is left alone in their apartment, methodically forging love letters from her to himself, each one more physically perfect and emotionally empty than the last.

narrative_beats:
# Seven Structural Beats for *The Forged Letters of Grigori Plink*

---

## Beat 1: The Counterfeiter's Perspective and the Town of Cabbage

**What Must Happen:** Introduce Grigori mid-forgery — hunched over a worktable, squinting through terrible eyesight at a tax stamp he is producing with painstaking, loving craftsmanship that is nonetheless laughably, obviously wrong. Establish the town: its smell, its architecture of thwarted ambition, its bureaucratic ecosystem. Establish Grigori's narrating voice — which catalogs his own bruises and injuries with the clinical specificity of a man filing insurance claims against the physical world. Something must go wrong physically in the very first scene: he ruins the stamp, or knocks over the ink, or falls off his stool. The clumsiness is not incidental. It is constitutive.

**Narrative Technique to Deploy:** *First-person unreliable self-assessment disguised as meticulous honesty.* Grigori must narrate with the precision of someone who notices every contusion, every splinter, every stair tread that betrayed him — while being entirely incapable of perceiving the larger structures (legal, romantic, political) closing around him. His myopia is literal and metaphorical simultaneously. He can see the hairline details of a forged stamp. He cannot see what anyone thinks of him. The bruise-cataloguing voice should read like a forensic report written by the corpse.

**Why This Beat Must Work:** The entire story depends on the reader accepting a specific contract: *the narrator's physical specificity is a substitute for emotional insight.* Grigori does not tell us what he feels. He tells us what hit him, where, how hard, and what sound it made. The reader must learn, in this opening beat, to translate impact into emotion — to understand that when Grigori says "I struck the doorframe at a velocity I estimate to have been considerable, given the acoustic properties of the resulting damage to the plaster," he is saying *I am a person the world keeps rejecting.* If this translation fails, the ending will not land. If it succeeds, the ending will be annihilating.

**What Makes It Structurally Load-Bearing:** This beat must also establish that Grigori's forgeries are *terrible* but also *laborious* — that he pours genuine artisanal care into products that fool no one. This is the story's foundational irony: the counterfeiter whose work is authentic (in effort, in devotion) but fake (in product, in result). That irony must be visible here so that when it inverts at the end — love letters that are technically perfect but emotionally counterfeit — the reader can feel the full structural rotation.

---

## Beat 2: The First Collision with Yevgenia

**What Must Happen:** Grigori must physically crash into Yevgenia. Not metaphorically. He must literally collide with her — through a door, down a corridor, off a landing — in a municipal building where she has just arrived as the new forensic documents clerk. The collision must be catastrophic to his body and to some piece of government property. Critically, the reader must learn two things about Yevgenia through Grigori's myopic lens: (1) she has been assigned specifically to analyze his forged tax stamps, and (2) something about her reaction to the collision is *wrong* — she does not respond with the disgust or irritation the town has trained him to expect. He registers this as data without understanding it. She finds him charming. He records only that she did not file a complaint.

**Narrative Technique to Deploy:** *Romantic interest perceived as bureaucratic anomaly.* Grigori should narrate Yevgenia's warmth as an irregularity in the system — a form filed incorrectly, a procedure that deviates from established protocol. He does not recognize attraction (hers or his own). He recognizes the absence of expected hostility, and it confuses him the way a forger would be confused by a banknote with no watermark. His language for her should borrow the vocabulary of his craft: her features are described the way he would describe the quality of paper stock or the viscosity of ink.

**Why This Beat Must Work:** This is the scene that establishes the story's central double-bind: Yevgenia is both the person most qualified to destroy him (she analyzes forged documents) and the person who will choose not to. The collision must literalize this: two trajectories that should result in mutual destruction instead producing something else. Every subsequent collision — and there must be several — will recapitulate this structure. The reader must feel, from this first impact, that Grigori and Yevgenia are on a collision course in every possible sense, and that the collisions are the relationship.

**What Makes It Structurally Load-Bearing:** The word "collision" must begin accumulating meanings here. Physical (slapstick), professional (investigator meets criminal), romantic (two people crashing into each other's lives). By the story's end, "collision" will also mean *complicity* and *destruction.* This beat is the first fork — the moment where Yevgenia could report him and doesn't — and the reader must feel both paths: the story where she files the report and the story where she doesn't.

---

## Beat 3: The Courtship Across Crime Scenes

**What Must Happen:** A compressed sequence — the structural equivalent of a montage, but narrated — in which Grigori and Yevgenia's relationship escalates through a series of encounters, each one located at a site of his criminality (his workshop, the tax office, a municipal archive) or her professional duty (evidence rooms, inspection desks, filing halls). Each encounter contains a romantic milestone — a first shared meal, a first tentative confidence, an almost-touch — immediately obliterated by slapstick catastrophe. The disasters must escalate in scale and absurdity. But beneath the escalation, each scene must also deposit a small, quiet detail of genuine tenderness that Grigori records without recognizing its significance.

**Narrative Technique to Deploy:** *Slapstick as displaced intimacy.* The physical comedy must function as the story's substitute for love scenes. Grigori cannot narrate emotional vulnerability — it is outside the resolution of his perceptual equipment. But he can narrate, in granular detail, the exact trajectory of his body as it falls *toward* or *into* or *through* something in Yevgenia's vicinity. Each pratfall is a declaration he doesn't know he's making. The technique is to let the reader feel the romance happening *inside* the slapstick rather than *despite* it — to make the destruction and the attraction formally indistinguishable.

**Why This Beat Must Work:** This is the section where the reader must fall in love with the couple, and the only available means are catastrophe and bureaucratic proximity. The tenderness must live in the margins of the physical comedy: in the fact that Yevgenia starts quietly moving breakable objects out of Grigori's path, in the way she begins filing his evidence reports with small clerical errors that make them harder to process, in her increasingly creative misfiling of his forged stamps into folders marked INCONCLUSIVE. The reader must understand that her love is expressed through deliberate professional negligence — the document clerk who forges omissions on behalf of the forger — so that Beat 6's exposure of her complicity arrives as both inevitable and heartbreaking.

**What Makes It Structurally Load-Bearing:** This beat is the story's engine, and it must establish the **formal equation that governs the entire narrative: every act of love in this story is also an act of forgery.** Yevgenia conceals, misfiles, overlooks. Grigori forges, fabricates, counterfeits. Their courtship is a collaborative fraud. This equation must be assembled here, unobtrusively, so that the ending — Grigori forging letters from her — reads not as a new behavior but as the logical terminal point of a pattern that was always present.

---

## Beat 4: The First Kiss Through the Filing Cabinet (Structural Midpoint)

**What Must Happen:** A single extended scene — the story's centrepiece — in which Grigori and Yevgenia are alone together and the accumulated romantic tension finally discharges. The kiss (or its attempt) must be narrated in Grigori's language of physical forensics: angles of approach, points of contact, estimated force. And it must be destroyed — immediately — by a slapstick disaster of the highest order: he tumbles backward through a filing cabinet full of evidence against him, scattering his own forged documents across the floor. The two of them must be on their hands and knees gathering the evidence of his guilt, and this must become, somehow, the most intimate scene in the story.

**Narrative Technique to Deploy:** *The slapstick catastrophe as structural pivot.* Up to this point, the physical disasters have been interruptions — comedy that disrupts romance. In this scene, the disaster must *become* the romance. The filing cabinet collapses, evidence scatters, and instead of the expected consequences (exposure, arrest, humiliation), what follows is Yevgenia on the floor beside him, handling his forgeries with something Grigori can only describe as care. He recognizes, dimly and for the first time, that she already knows. She has always known. The scene must end with both of them surrounded by the material proof of his criminality, and with the unspoken understanding that she has chosen him over her professional duty.

**Why This Beat Must Work:** This is the story's midpoint reversal, and it reverses not the plot but the *reader's understanding of the central relationship.* Before this scene, we could believe Yevgenia was oblivious, charmed, fooled. After this scene, we know she is complicit — eyes open, choosing freely. This transforms the love story from comedy into something with real moral weight. She is not a fool. She is an accomplice. And that distinction is what gives Beat 6 its teeth: the bureaucratic machinery does not punish her for being naive. It punishes her for choosing love over duty, which is an entirely different kind of tragedy.

**What Makes It Structurally Load-Bearing:** The filing cabinet full of evidence functions as the story's version of Borges's labyrinth: a structure that contains all possible outcomes simultaneously. While the documents are scattered on the floor, every possible future is present — the one where she reports him, the one where they flee, the one where they laugh and nothing changes. Yevgenia picking up the pages and choosing to put them back *out of order* is her act of authorship, her choice of which fork to follow. The story must let the reader feel the weight of that choice before moving on.

---

## Beat 5: The Accidental Heroism

**What Must Happen:** Grigori's forgeries — inept, obvious, lovingly crafted — must accidentally expose a genuine crime: the deputy governor's massive pension fraud. The mechanism should be absurd and precise: his counterfeit tax stamps, when compared against the "genuine" ones filed by the deputy governor's office, reveal that the *genuine* stamps are themselves forgeries, but competent ones. Grigori's bad fakes expose someone else's good fakes. His failure as a criminal becomes his success as an inadvertent whistleblower. The town celebrates him. There is a banquet. The mayor pins a medal on his chest. He topples into something at the ceremony. Yevgenia watches from a seat in the audience, and for the first time in the story, he registers something on her face that he cannot catalog as any known physical phenomenon. (It is fear.)

**Narrative Technique to Deploy:** *Ironic elevation as structural trap.* The celebration must be narrated by Grigori with the same bruise-cataloguing detachment he brings to everything, which means the reader feels the dramatic irony he cannot: this is not a reward. It is exposure. By making Grigori publicly visible — a hero, celebrated, examined — the town's attention turns toward the full apparatus of his life, including the forensic clerk who was supposed to have caught him earlier and didn't. The medal scene must feel, to the reader, like a noose being fitted to both their necks while the crowd applauds.

**Why This Beat Must Work:** This is the story's cruelest structural joke, and it must land as both comedy *and* foreboding simultaneously. The reader must laugh at the absurdity — a terrible counterfeiter accidentally exposing a real fraud — while feeling dread pool beneath the laughter. The technique is tonal double-exposure: every sentence in the banquet scene must function as celebration on its surface and as countdown underneath. Grigori's description of the medal's weight on his chest should echo, faintly, his earlier descriptions of injuries.

**What Makes It Structurally Load-Bearing:** This beat introduces the story's critical thematic proposition: **the town does not love Grigori. The town loves the** ***idea*** **of an honest man.** The moment Grigori becomes useful to the town's self-narrative — *we rooted out corruption! one of our own discovered the fraud!* — he is absorbed into a story that has no room for who he actually is. This is forgery at the civic level: the town counterfeits a hero out of a criminal. And like all forgeries in this story, it will not survive close inspection. The pension-fraud exposure is the mechanism that elevates Grigori, but what it *structurally* does is make Yevgenia's misfiling visible to anyone who looks. The same light that makes him a hero makes her a criminal.

---

## Beat 6: The Bureaucratic Annihilation

**What Must Happen:** The exposure arrives not as a dramatic confrontation but as paperwork. An audit. A review. A clerk in a different office notices the irregularities in Yevgenia's filing of Grigori's case — the misfiled evidence, the reports marked INCONCLUSIVE, the missing pages. (Missing pages: the same device Borges uses in his opening. Here, the absence that framed the story becomes the absence that destroys the characters.) The discovery is reported up the chain. There is no villain. The system simply processes the information. Yevgenia is transferred to a records office in a city so obscure no one can find it on a map — a place that may not exist, a bureaucratic oubliette. There is no trial, no public shaming, no dramatic scene. The machinery that briefly loved Grigori now grinds them both with the same indifference with which it once celebrated him. Their secret wedding — which should receive its own brief, devastating flashback here, ending with Grigori face-first in the registrar's ink pot — is functionally annulled by institutional geography.

**Narrative Technique to Deploy:** *Systemic violence narrated as procedural routine.* Grigori must recount the destruction of his marriage and Yevgenia's exile in the same flat, inventory-like voice he uses for his injuries. But the reader, who has by now learned to translate his physical language into emotional content, will feel the enormity of what he is suppressing. The transfer orders, the reassignment papers, the official correspondence — these must be narrated with the meticulous attention Grigori normally reserves for describing the angle at which he struck a banister. The effect should be that bureaucratic language becomes the story's most violent register: more devastating than any slapstick fall, because this time nothing is funny
narrative_story:
# The Forged Letters of Grigori Plink

## I.

The ink was wrong. I will state this plainly, as I state all things, because precision is the only courtesy a man can extend to a world that has otherwise shown him none. The ink was wrong: too thin by perhaps a twentieth of a degree on the viscometric scale I have developed through years of practice, a scale I keep in a notebook whose spine has been repaired eleven times with fish glue and whose pages smell, as does everything in this town, of cabbage.

The town is called Volsky. It is not on most maps, and the maps on which it does appear tend to depict it with a reluctance that suggests the cartographer was fulfilling an obligation rather than recording a discovery. The buildings are the color that occurs when ambition fails to become paint. They lean. They lean the way I lean, which is to say persistently and in directions that alarm structural engineers. The central administrative district consists of fourteen buildings arranged around a square that has never once, in my observation, been geometrically square, and the primary economic activities are the processing of cabbage, the filing of documents related to the processing of cabbage, and the generation of supplementary documents to correct errors in the original documents related to the processing of cabbage.

I have lived here for the entirety of my thirty-seven years. I have sustained, in that time, fractures to the left wrist (twice), the right clavicle, the fourth and seventh ribs on the left side, the second toe of the right foot (three times; the same toe; I have come to regard it as an antagonist), the orbital bone above the left eye, and the nose (a number I have lost count of and will estimate conservatively at six). I have received contusions beyond meaningful enumeration. I mention these not for sympathy — a resource I have never successfully applied for — but as context for the events I am about to relate, and as evidence that the physical world has maintained, with respect to my body, a consistent editorial policy of rejection.

On the morning in question — a Tuesday, I believe, though the days in Volsky tend to present themselves with an institutional sameness that makes such determinations approximate — I was seated at my worktable in the room above the laundry on Kropotkinskaya Street, producing a tax stamp for the district cabbage levy. I had been working on it for eleven days. This may seem excessive for a stamp whose legitimate counterpart is produced, I am told, by a mechanical press in four seconds, but I do not have a mechanical press. I have a magnifying lens with a crack down its center that bisects whatever I examine into two offset halves, a set of nibs I carved myself from goose quills donated — which is to say discarded — by the woman downstairs who operates the laundry, a pot of ink I mixed from lampblack and linseed oil according to a recipe I found in a water-damaged pamphlet, and my hands, which are precise in the way that a clock is precise when it tells the wrong time with absolute consistency.

I should say something about my eyes. They are, by any ophthalmological standard, a disaster. I was examined once, at age fourteen, by a traveling optician who passed through Volsky under the mistaken impression that it was a different town. He held lenses before me and asked what I could see, and I described, with the accuracy that is my only reliable trait, the exact character and quality of the blur. He told me I needed spectacles of a prescription he was not equipped to provide. He suggested I travel to Moscow. I have not traveled to Moscow. Moscow is, by my best estimate, nine hundred kilometers from Volsky, and I have calculated, based on my frequency of injurious incidents per kilometer traveled on foot — a figure I arrived at after keeping careful records during a trip to the post office, a distance of two hundred meters, during which I sustained a bruise to the left shin (curb), an abrasion to both palms (icy step), and a laceration of the right ear (low-hanging shop sign, metal) — that I would arrive in Moscow as a medical specimen rather than a patient.

So I see the way I see: at very close range, with hallucinatory sharpness, every fiber and flaw and grain of surface magnified into a landscape I can navigate with my fingertips as much as my eyes. And at any distance beyond the length of my arm, the world becomes a negotiation between smears of color whose intentions toward me I must infer from past experience, which has taught me that their intentions are generally hostile.

This is why I am good at what I do. Or rather — I must be honest; I am always honest, which is an unusual trait in a forger and may go some distance toward explaining my difficulties — this is why I am *devoted* to what I do. Whether I am *good* at it is a question I have found it more productive not to examine.

The tax stamp. I was applying the final detail — the small imperialist eagle that perches in the upper left corner of all district fiscal documents, a bird I have rendered so many times I could draw it from memory even if my memory, like my eyesight, were not to be trusted — when my elbow, acting on its own recognizance, as my joints often do, struck the inkpot.

The inkpot did not merely fall. It executed a quarter-rotation on the edge of the table that I would describe, were I inclined toward metaphor, which I am not, as balletic. It hung for a duration I estimate at one-third of a second — long enough for me to observe, with the close-range clarity that is my single gift, the way the meniscus of the ink trembled at the lip of the vessel, a perfect black dome of surface tension containing the full record of eleven days' work in negative, the way a puddle contains the sky. Then the surface tension failed, as surfaces in my vicinity invariably do, and the ink fell.

It fell onto the stamp.

It fell onto the table.

It fell onto the chair, because I had lunged for the inkpot and in doing so pitched the chair sideways, and then it fell onto me, because I had fallen after the chair, and the floor of the room above the laundry on Kropotkinskaya Street, which slopes seventeen degrees toward the eastern wall due to a subsidence I have reported to the building's owner four times without acknowledgment, carried me in a gentle slide until my head struck the baseboard with a force sufficient to produce a sound I would characterize as *tonal* — a resonant, almost musical report that suggested the baseboard was hollow, which explained the draft.

I lay on the floor. The ink was on my face, in my hair, pooling in the depression of my left ear. The stamp, eleven days in the making, was obliterated. Above me, on the table's edge, I could see, with what remained of my upward vision, the magnifying lens with its cracked meridian gazing down at me like the eye of a god who has examined his creation and found the work not even worth the trouble of destroying properly.

I sat up. I catalogued: a contusion to the occipital region, already swelling to a diameter I estimated at three centimeters; ink in the left ear canal, which produced a sensation of distant, muffled roaring, as though the sea had been filed in the wrong department and was trying to find its way out; a stiffness in the lower back consistent with having become briefly airborne; the taste of lampblack and linseed, which I mention only because it is relevant to note that this is the taste of my life's work, and it is not good.

I began again.

This is, I think, the essential fact about me, and I offer it without commentary: I began again. I took a fresh sheet of paper — my fourth-to-last sheet; paper is expensive and I am not — and I positioned it on the table, and I leaned close, so close my breath made the paper shiver, and I began to draw the eagle again, one feather at a time, with the devotion of a monk illuminating a manuscript that no one will read in a language no one speaks for a God whose existence is, at best, *under review*.

The resulting stamp, when I completed it four days later, was, like all my stamps, a work of sincere and total effort. The eagle's feathers were individually rendered with a delicacy that, examined under magnification, revealed a quality of attention bordering on the devotional. The border filigree was hand-drawn in strokes so fine they might have been the work of a spider who had studied calligraphy. The serial number was invented but plausible. The district seal was a faithful reproduction of memory, which is to say it was faithful to what I remembered, and what I remembered was faithful to what I had seen, and what I had seen was faithful to what my eyes were capable of delivering, which introduces into the chain of fidelity a link of such catastrophic weakness that the wonder is not that my stamps fail to convince but that they are recognizable as stamps at all.

I say all this not as self-deprecation but as inventory. A man should know what he has. I have: two hands, steady at close range, that shake beyond it. Eyes that magnify what is near and abolish what is far. A body that the physical world treats as a rough draft. A room above a laundry. And a craft I practice with the fidelity of a priest and the success rate of a heretic.

This was my life in Volsky on the morning before the morning I met Yevgenia Fyodorovna Raskova, and it seems necessary to have established it completely, because what followed was a sequence of events that, like the inkpot, began with a small disturbance of equilibrium and ended with everything I had made — every careful, fraudulent, devoted thing — facedown on the floor.

---

## II.

The Municipal Bureau of Fiscal Documents occupies the third floor of a building on the east side of the square that I believe was originally designed as something else — a school, perhaps, or a granary — and was converted to bureaucratic use with the same enthusiasm the town brings to all its conversions, which is to say the walls were painted a different color and a sign was hung and everyone agreed to pretend.

I was there because my stamps, once completed, must be introduced into the fiscal ecosystem, which requires that I visit the bureau, present a cabbage tax document to which the stamp has been affixed, and submit it to the clerk on duty for processing. The clerk on duty has, for as long as I have been conducting this enterprise, been a man named Pyotr Afanasyevich, whose capacity for visual discernment I have estimated, through extensive empirical observation, to be roughly equivalent to mine — which is to say he can perceive what is directly in front of his nose, and everything beyond that falls into the category of *somebody else's problem*. Pyotr Afanasyevich has processed my stamps for four years without incident, which I attribute not to the quality of my forgeries but to the quality of his indifference, a resource so vast and so consistently renewable that it constitutes, in my view, the only truly sustainable industry in Volsky.

I was ascending the staircase to the third floor. The staircase has forty-one steps. I know this because I have counted them on each of my visits, and because I have fallen on, by my records, fourteen distinct steps across thirty-seven visits, giving a failure rate of approximately one injurious step per 2.6 visits, or what I have privately designated a *Plink coefficient* suitable for any staircase I am likely to encounter.

On this particular morning, I had reached step thirty-eight — the final landing, where the staircase turns — when the door at the top of the stairs opened outward. I should note that this door has always opened outward, a design choice I have questioned in several unsubmitted letters to the building commission, because a door that opens outward at the top of a staircase is not a door. It is a trebuchet.

The door opened. I was on step thirty-eight, which placed my face at the precise altitude of the door's central panel. What followed occupied, by my reconstruction, approximately one and one-quarter seconds, but I will render it with the fidelity it deserves, because it was the most consequential one and one-quarter seconds of my life, and because the details — the specific physical details — are the only language I have for what happened.

The door struck me on the forehead, slightly left of center, at a point I later measured to be four centimeters above the left eyebrow. The force was sufficient to arrest my forward momentum and initiate a rearward momentum, which, given my position on step thirty-eight of a staircase that turns at that point, translated into a lateral displacement that the staircase's architecture was not designed to accommodate. My left hand seized the banister. The banister, which I have previously noted in my unsubmitted letters as being secured by screws that appeared to predate the concept of maintenance, separated from the wall with a groan that I can only describe as *sympathetic*, as though the banister had been waiting for a legitimate reason to abandon its post and I had finally provided one.

I fell. The direction of the fall was complex. I will say only that it involved a rotational component that brought my back into contact with three risers and my right knee into contact with the wall, and that the banister, still in my grip, accompanied me with the loyalty of a companion animal, swinging in an arc that terminated against a window on the half-landing, which did not break but produced a sound — a deep, almost ecclesiastical hum — that seemed, in retrospect, like the building's attempt at a wedding bell.

I came to rest on the half-landing between floors two and three, supine, the banister across my chest like a ceremonial staff, plaster dust settling on my face. And framed in the doorway above me, silhouetted against the fluorescent light of the third-floor corridor, was a shape.

I could not see its features. It was at doorway distance, which placed it beyond the horizon of my useful vision. It was a smear. But it was — I noted this with the diagnostic attention I bring to all sensory data — a smear of a quality I had not previously encountered. The fluorescent light behind it produced a diffraction I can only describe as *warm*, though I am aware that fluorescent light is, by its physical nature, the opposite of warm, and that the warmth I perceived must therefore have originated in the shape itself, or else in the contusion to my forehead, which was already producing visual effects I was not in a position to attribute with scientific confidence.

"Oh," said the shape. Its voice was — I will describe what I can verify — in a register approximately two octaves above my own, with a quality I would characterize, using the vocabulary of my craft, as *linen*: a smooth texture with a fine, discernible grain.

"I have fallen," I said, because this seemed both evident and worth confirming.

The shape descended toward me. This was alarming, because things that descend toward me are generally in the process of striking me, and I braced accordingly — a motion that caused the banister to roll off my chest and clatter down the remaining steps to the second-floor landing with a percussive enthusiasm I might have admired under other circumstances. But the shape, as it approached, did not strike me. It came close enough to enter the field of my useful vision, and then — in an act of focal mercy I had never before experienced — it came *closer*, and the smear resolved, and I saw a face.

I will describe it the way I describe all things: as surfaces.

The skin had the consistency of good paper — not the pressed municipal stock I use for stamps, which is porous and receives ink reluctantly, but something finer, something with a thread count, if paper can be said to have a thread count. The eyes were a color I could not determine with confidence because the fluorescent light above was contaminating my readings, but they were large, and they were, at this range — she had knelt beside me, she was very close — examining me with an attention I recognized. It was the attention I bring to a document I am about to reproduce: close, investigative, noting every flaw.

I flinched. People do not look at me. People look at the space I have recently vacated, usually because I have fallen out of it.

"You are bleeding," she said, in that linen voice.

I reached up and touched my forehead. She was correct. "A laceration," I said. "Approximately three centimeters. Superficial. The bleeding is" — I consulted the flow rate against

Form 27-B: Application for Continued Existence

Seventeen years after the Auditors—vast bureaucratic entities that “processed” every civilization that achieved interstellar travel—reduced humanity to a single colony ship, the 3,000 survivors discover they've been filing the wrong forms. The ship's journey to a rumored sanctuary planet becomes an absurdist odyssey through cosmic red tape: the Auditors aren't malevolent, they're just following procedures established by a precursor civilization they also accidentally “archived” due to a clerical error millennia ago. Our omniscient narrator follows multiple characters—a former DMV employee who becomes humanity's unlikely advocate, a child who keeps drawing pictures that somehow constitute valid appeals, a captain who refuses to accept that the universe runs on triplicate—as they navigate waiting rooms that exist outside spacetime, submit applications for “Species Continuity Extensions,” and slowly realize the sanctuary planet requires a permit that was discontinued in the previous cosmic fiscal cycle. The light drama emerges from humanity's stubborn, warmly ridiculous insistence on treating existential annihilation as a customer service issue that can be resolved if they just speak to the right manager.
